title: From script to tool: parameters
summary: Turn a hard-coded script into a tool: param() with types, defaults and Mandatory, validation attributes, CmdletBinding and -Verbose, comment-based help, and splatting.

steps.title: param() and [CmdletBinding()]
body: A script or function becomes a real tool when its inputs are **parameters** instead of variables edited by hand:
- **Types** (`[string]`, `[int]`, `[datetime]`, `[string[]]` for a list) convert input for you and reject nonsense:
`-Top ten` fails at once with a clear message.
- **`Mandatory`** makes PowerShell ask for the value interactively, and **fail** in a non-interactive run
(`pwsh -NonInteractive`, a scheduled task), which is what you want there.
- **`[CmdletBinding()]`** makes it an *advanced* script or function: it gets the common parameters (`-Verbose`,
`-Debug`, `-ErrorAction`, `-WarningAction`, `-OutVariable`, ...) and rejects parameters it does not know.
`Write-Verbose` messages appear only when the caller passes `-Verbose`. (A `[Parameter(...)]` attribute on any
parameter has the same effect; write `[CmdletBinding()]` anyway, so readers see it.)
The same `param()` block works at the top of a `.ps1` file (run it with `./Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path ...`) and as the

steps.prompt: What does adding `[CmdletBinding()]` above `param()` give a script, with no other change?
options: The common parameters such as `-Verbose`, `-ErrorAction` and `-WarningAction`, and an error for unknown parameters
Automatic `-WhatIf` support on every command inside it
steps.explain: Without it, a script silently ignores `-Verbose` and collects any unknown arguments in `$args`, so a typo such as `-Unti GB` is ignored. `-WhatIf` needs `SupportsShouldProcess` as well (next lesson).

steps.title: Validation attributes: refuse bad input up front
body: Validation runs **before** the body, so a bad value never gets halfway through a clean-up:
| `[ValidateSet('KB', 'MB', 'GB')]` | anything not in the list (and gives Tab completion for free) |
| `[ValidatePattern('^[A-Z]{3}-\d+$')]` | strings that do not match the regex |
| `[ValidateScript({ Test-Path -LiteralPath $_ -PathType Container })]` | anything for which the script block is not `$true` |
| `[ValidateCount(1, 5)]` | arrays with too few or too many items |
The error names the parameter and the rule, for example *Cannot validate argument on parameter 'Unit'. The argument
"TB" does not belong to the set "KB,MB,GB"*. That message is the user documentation for free.

steps.title: Parameters for the disk-usage script
prompt: `~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1` lists the biggest files, but the folder, the count and the unit are hard-coded. Make
them parameters, so this works: `~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path ~/data -Top 3 -Unit GB`.
- **`-Path`**: mandatory, and it must be an **existing folder**;
Keep the output: objects with `Name` and `Size` (the size in the chosen unit, rounded to one decimal).
Edit it on the page with `nano ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1`, or write it with a here-string and `Set-Content`.

checks.name: -Top 3 -Unit MB
checks.fail: `-Path ~/data -Top 3 -Unit MB` should give the three biggest files with their size in MB.

checks.name: defaults: -Top 10, -Unit MB; and KB works
checks.fail: Without `-Top`, `-Path ~` should return 10 files; without `-Unit` sizes are in MB (`11`); with `-Unit KB` the biggest is `11264`.

checks.name: -Unit TB is refused
checks.expectContains: does not belong to the set
checks.fail: `-Unit TB` should be refused by a `[ValidateSet(...)]`.

checks.name: -Top 0 and -Top 500 are refused
checks.cmd: a=$(pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path ~/data -Top 0 2>&1); b=$(pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path ~/data -Top 500 2>&1); echo "$a" | grep -q 'Cannot validate argument' && echo "$b" | grep -q 'Cannot validate argument'
checks.fail: `-Top 0` and `-Top 500` should both be refused by a `[ValidateRange(1, 100)]`.

checks.name: a missing folder or no -Path fails
checks.cmd: pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path ~/no-such-folder >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 1; pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 1; pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path ~/data/notes.md >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 1; exit 0
checks.fail: The script must fail (non-zero exit) when `-Path` is missing, does not exist, or is a file rather than a folder.

hints: Start the file with a `param( ... )` block and delete the `$Path = ...` and `$Top = ...` lines.
For the unit, look up the divisor: `$divisor = @{ KB = 1KB; MB = 1MB; GB = 1GB }[$Unit]`, and divide by `$divisor` instead of `1MB`.
steps.explain: The script still outputs **objects**, not formatted text, so a caller can sort, filter or export them: `./Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path D:\ -Top 50 | Export-Csv big-files.csv`. That is the difference between a script and a tool.

steps.title: Help for your own tools, and splatting
body: **Comment-based help** at the top of a script (or inside a function) makes `Get-Help` work for it, examples and all:
Lists the biggest files under a folder.
The folder to scan, including subfolders.
**Splatting** passes a hashtable of parameters with `@` instead of `$`. Long calls become readable, and you can
Inside an advanced function, **`$PSBoundParameters`** is a hashtable of exactly the parameters the caller passed,

steps.explain: The hashtable is built with `@{ }`; it is passed with `@request` (at sign, not dollar). Each key becomes `-Key value`; a `$true` value for a switch, like `Recurse = $true`, becomes `-Recurse`.

steps.title: Help and -Verbose for the tool
prompt: `~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1` now has parameters. Make it self-explaining:
1. comment-based help at the top with a **`.SYNOPSIS`** and at least one **`.EXAMPLE`** that calls the script with `-Path`,
2. **`[CmdletBinding()]`** above `param(`, and a `Write-Verbose` line that prints **`Scanning <path>`** before it scans,

checks.name: Get-Help shows a synopsis
checks.fail: `(Get-Help ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1).Synopsis` should be your one-line description, not just the syntax line. Put a `<# .SYNOPSIS ... #>` block at the very top.

checks.name: Get-Help -Examples shows an example with -Path
checks.fail: Add an `.EXAMPLE` section whose first line calls `Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Path ...`.

checks.name: -Verbose says what it scans
checks.fail: With `-Verbose`, the script should print `VERBOSE: Scanning /home/learner/data` (or the path as given). Needs `[CmdletBinding()]` and `Write-Verbose`.

checks.name: quiet without -Verbose, same output
checks.fail: Without `-Verbose`, the script should only output its two result objects.

hints: Comment-based help goes first in the file: `<#`, `.SYNOPSIS`, a line of text, `.EXAMPLE`, an example line, `#>`. Then `[CmdletBinding()]`, then `param(`.

Easiest: read the file, put the new top in front: `$body = Get-Content ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Raw`, then `Set-Content ~/scripts/Get-DiskUsage.ps1 -Value ($header + $body.Replace('$divisor =', "Write-Verbose `"Scanning `$Path`"`n`$divisor ="))`, where `$header` is a here-string with the help and `[CmdletBinding()]`.
solution: Lists the biggest files under a folder, with their size in KB, MB or GB.
The folder to scan, including all subfolders.
steps.explain: `Write-Verbose` is the right channel for "what am I doing" messages: silent by default, visible with `-Verbose`, and it never pollutes the output objects. The same goes for `Write-Warning` (always shown, stream 3) and `Write-Debug` (with `-Debug`).

code: if ($Force) { "deploying to $Env, no questions" } else { "deploying to $Env" }
steps.explain: A parameter not passed takes its default; a `[switch]` is `$false` unless it is present. Switches should default to off: name them for the unusual behaviour (`-Force`, `-IncludeHidden`), never `-NoSomething = $true`.
